implementation_notes: NestJS's container instantiates the application service as an @Injectable() provider declared in a module, so constructor injection and module wiring replace manual composition, and the transaction is owned either by Prisma's interactive $transaction callback or by TypeORM's dataSource.transaction/QueryRunner handed to the repositories. What replaces the classic structure is the container plus decorator metadata; the service itself stays an ordinary class whose methods are the use cases, which also makes it the natural place for guards/interceptors for authorization and logging.
pitfalls: The interactive-transaction client (Prisma.TransactionClient) lacks $connect/$transaction; repositories must be written against that narrow type, and calling $transaction on it fails.
A repository that holds the root client bypasses the transaction - pass tx explicitly, or accept the implicit coupling of AsyncLocalStorage.
Providers are singletons by default, so per-request state in a service makes concurrent requests interfere; keep the service stateless or request-scoped.

variants.name: Framework-free use-case function with a Prisma interactive transaction
variants.idiom_name: exported async function taking its ports + prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)
variants.implementation_notes: Without a container the use case is a plain exported function whose collaborators are parameters (or module-level singletons created once at the composition root); the transaction is the same Prisma interactive $transaction callback and the ports are TypeScript interfaces typed on Prisma.TransactionClient. Choose it when the application is a small Fastify/Express service where a container would be ceremony: the function is directly unit-testable by passing fakes, and the dependency set of each use case is visible in its signature.
pitfalls: Without a container the composition root must wire and reuse one PrismaClient; constructing one per call destroys connection pooling.
Interfaces over Prisma.TransactionClient must be kept in sync with the generated client, or the port silently widens past the transaction type.
Interactive transactions default to a 5s timeout and a 2s acquire wait; long use cases need explicit options or they fail under load.
